3.3a — Fire Rate: Cooldowns & Time

In the previous lab, stepping in range triggered a continuous laser of 60 bullets every second. In software development, rate limiting is a fundamental problem: actions must not happen faster than a designated cadence. Today, you evaluate three different Unity timing functions and build a cooldown timer into TurretController.cs.

Read the Docs ~15 min

How do we make an object "wait" between actions in Unity? Because Update() executes every frame without stopping, we cannot use a blocking sleep function (which would freeze the entire game window!). Instead, game engines offer three common patterns for timing:

Timing ApproachMechanismHow It Works
1. Time.time Timestamp if (Time.time >= lastTime + cooldown) Records the absolute game time when an action occurred. Checks if the clock has advanced enough since the timestamp.
2. Countdown Variable timer -= Time.deltaTime; Decrements a float variable each frame. Fires when the counter reaches zero, then resets.
3. Coroutines yield return new WaitForSeconds(cooldown); Pauses a method execution asynchronously and resumes after a specified number of seconds without blocking the engine.

Socratic: Evaluating Timing Approaches

  1. Why is the Time.time timestamp method particularly clean for single, independent actions like firing a shot or checking player damage?
  2. In what scenarios are Coroutines significantly more powerful than checking timestamps in Update()? (Hint: Imagine designing a boss attack that charges a laser for 1.5s, fires 5 rapid shots 0.2s apart, and then rests for 3s.)
  3. What happens if you use a local variable inside Update() for a timer instead of a class field? Why must timers live as member variables of the class?
Analyze the Architecture ~15 min

Examine how an industrial laser cutter uses compound boolean logic and timestamp tracking to prevent hardware overheating: 

using UnityEngine;

// Industrial tool managing pulse intervals via timestamp gating
public class LaserDrill : MonoBehaviour
{
    // Designer knob: delay required between pulses
    [SerializeField] private float pulseCooldown = 1.5f;

    // Internal memory: timestamp of the previous discharge
    private float lastPulseTime = 0f;

    public void AttemptDischarge(bool sensorTargetAcquired)
    {
        // Compound condition: target is valid AND cooldown duration has elapsed
        if (sensorTargetAcquired && Time.time >= lastPulseTime + pulseCooldown)
        {
            FirePulse();

            // Reset the timestamp memory to current engine clock
            lastPulseTime = Time.time;
        }
    }

    private void FirePulse()
    {
        Debug.Log("Laser pulse discharged at: " + Time.time);
    }
}

Predict Before Building

  1. If lastPulseTime is 4.0 and pulseCooldown is 1.5, what is the earliest Time.time value at which Time.time >= lastPulseTime + pulseCooldown evaluates to true?
  2. In boolean logic, if sensorTargetAcquired is false, does Unity bother evaluating the right-hand side of the && operator? (This is called short-circuit evaluation).
Build Lab: Your Turn ~25 min
Architectural Specification for TurretController.cs:
  1. Cooldown Tuning Knob: Declare a serialized private float field named attackCooldown with a default value of 2f.
  2. Timestamp Memory: Declare a private float field named lastAttackTime initialized to 0f.
  3. Compound Gating in Update: In Update(), modify your attack conditional to require both conditions using &&:
    • The player must be within range: distanceToPlayer <= maxAttackRange.
    • AND enough time must have passed: Time.time >= lastAttackTime + attackCooldown.
  4. Reset Clock on Attack: Inside the if branch, call AttackPlayer();, and immediately record the current time by assigning lastAttackTime = Time.time;.

Save and return to Unity. Press Play and walk inside the turret's attack radius. Instead of a solid wall of bullets, the turret now fires a single projectile, pauses for 2 seconds, and then fires again!

Bug Hunt: Timer Faults

  1. What happens if you comment out the line updating lastAttackTime? Why does the turret revert back to firing 60 bullets per second?
  2. In the Inspector for Turret, change Attack Cooldown to 0.5. Test it in play mode. How does the encounter pacing change?
  3. What happens if you initialize private float lastAttackTime = 100f; in your code? When the game starts, how many seconds must you wait before the turret can take its very first shot?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Testing Countdown Timers

  1. Instead of timestamp checking with Time.time, try engineering a countdown timer using timer -= Time.deltaTime;. When timer <= 0f, fire and reset timer = attackCooldown;. Which timing approach feels cleaner to you?
  2. How could you use this exact same cooldown pattern to prevent the player from taking spike damage 60 times a second if they stand on a spike?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Compare three timing patterns in Unity (Time.time, countdown timers, Coroutines)
  • Construct a compound boolean conditional using &&
  • Explain why the timestamp reset line (lastAttackTime = Time.time) is mandatory
  • Tune a cooldown knob in the Inspector to balance game difficulty
  • Commit your fire rate cooldown system to GitHub
